Content:
In general, for [MATH: k>0,]

Content:
- the graph of [MATH: y=f(x-k)] is a horizontal translation of [MATH: y=f(x)] by [MATH: k] units to the right, while
- the graph of [MATH: y=f(x+k)] is a horizontal translation of [MATH: y=f(x)] by [MATH: k] units to the left.

Content:
Watch out! It may seem counterintuitive that subtracting [MATH: k] moves the graph to the right, while adding [MATH: k] moves the graph to the left. However, this is in fact true.

Content:
To see why, let's consider the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] shown below. Let's use this graph to plot the graph of [MATH: y=f(x-2).]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ab59bc3503a3bf712e3abafeda16d870]

Content:
Let's take some points on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] and find the corresponding points on the graphs of [MATH: y=f(x-2).]

Content:
For example, take the point [MATH: (3,-4).] The fact that it's on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] means that [MATH: f(3)=-4.] Then if [MATH: x={\color{red}5},] we have
[MATH: f(x-2) = f({\color{red}5}-2) = f(3) = -4,]
which means that [MATH: ({\color{red}5},-4)] is on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x-2).]

Content:
For each point on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] there is a corresponding point on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x-2)] with the same [MATH: y]-value and a [MATH: x]-value that is [MATH: 2] units greater! Several more examples of points are shown below.

Content:
[MATH: Points on [math]y=f(x)[/math]|Points on [math]y=f(x-2)[/math]; (3, − 4)|(5, − 4); (1, 2)|(3, 2); (0, 1.5)|(2, 1.5); (− 2, 0)|(0, 0)]

Content:
Now, let's plot both curves.

Graphic:

Content:
We see that every point on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x-2)] is shifted [MATH: 2] units to the right of the corresponding point on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x).]

items.title: Combining Vertical and Horizontal Translations

sections.normalized_html: When graphing a function, we can combine vertical and horizontal translations. In general, the graph of [MATH: y = f(x-h)+k] is a translation of the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] by [MATH: h] units to the right and [MATH: k] units up.
sections.readable_text:
When graphing a function, we can combine vertical and horizontal translations. In general, the graph of
[MATH: y = f(x-h)+k]
is a translation of the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] by [MATH: h] units to the right and [MATH: k] units up.

sections.normalized_html: It doesn't matter which translation we do first, but it's often easiest to start with the horizontal translation.
sections.readable_text: It doesn't matter which translation we do first, but it's often easiest to start with the horizontal translation.

items.readable_text:
Content:
When graphing a function, we can combine vertical and horizontal translations. In general, the graph of
[MATH: y = f(x-h)+k]
is a translation of the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] by [MATH: h] units to the right and [MATH: k] units up.

Content:
It doesn't matter which translation we do first, but it's often easiest to start with the horizontal translation.
